source: Kahneman, Sibony, Sunstein (2021) Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (via Wikipedia summary page; book itself not opened)
finding: Founding noise audit. Underwriters at an insurer priced the same five fictive customers. Prices differed far more than managers expected.
numbers: Median premiums varied by 55%, about five times what underwriters and executives expected (Wikipedia summary of the book).
limits: Secondary source. The book text was not opened. Single firm, fictive cases.
agent_relevance: Same input, different judge, very different output. Our agent samples are 'judges'. Expect and measure this spread; do not trust one sample.

source: Kahneman, Sibony, Sunstein (2021) Noise - definitions of noise types (via Wikipedia summary page)
finding: Three kinds of noise: level noise (judges differ in overall strictness), stable pattern noise (a judge reacts to particular case features in a lasting way), occasion noise (mood and other passing factors). Cutting noise by a given amount cuts total error as much as cutting bias by that amount.
numbers: Error is described as bias plus noise. The book's equation (from memory, not on the page read): mean squared error = bias squared + system noise squared; system noise squared = level noise squared + pattern noise squared.
limits: Equation not shown on the page read; stated from memory of the book. Critics (Gelman, Ortmann, Blastland) say the concept is not new; Donohoe says less noise can mean more rigidity.
agent_relevance: Gives a vocabulary. Level noise = model-wide leaning; pattern noise = prompt/case interaction; occasion noise = sampling randomness. Each needs its own fix.

source: Kahneman, Sibony, Sunstein (2021) Noise - other noise studies cited (via Wikipedia summary page)
finding: Many professions show large unwanted spread between judges.
numbers: 208 judges, 16 fictive cases: unanimous prison recommendation in only 3 cases; one case averaged 1.1 years but one judge gave 15. 682 real admissions decisions: weighting shifted with cloudy vs sunny days. Two psychiatrists diagnosed 426 hospital patients and agreed on the illness in only half. Radiologists: some never missed breast cancer, others missed half; false positives ranged 1% to 64%. Interview meta-analysis: panel members disagreed on best candidate a quarter of the time.
limits: Second-hand summary. Weather and birthday effects rest on single studies not independently confirmed in the page read.
agent_relevance: Spread appears even in trained experts, so 'a strong judge' is not a cure. Aggregate and check.

source: Kahneman, Rosenfield, Gandhi, Blaser (2016) Noise: How to overcome the high, hidden cost of inconsistent decision making. Harvard Business Review
finding: Short public form of the noise audit idea. Only the lede and summary were readable (paywall). A customer sent the same application to two offices of a financial firm and got very different quotes.
numbers: No figures readable on the open page.
quote: Judgments can vary a great deal from one individual to the next, even when people are in the ...
limits: Paywalled. Full numbers could not be checked in the primary article.
agent_relevance: Motivates a noise audit of our own agent: run the same item many times and compare.

source: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig, Mullainathan (2017/2018) Human decisions and machine predictions (NBER 23180)
finding: Bail judges in New York City. A model trained on case data ranks defendants better than judges do. Part of the judge error is noise: a model of the judge's own past decisions beats the judge.
numbers: 554,689 cases (80% train = 443,751). Model AUC 0.707. At the judges' own release rate: 24.7% fewer crimes; at the judges' own crime rate: 41.8% fewer people jailed (abstract: up to 24.8% and 42.0%). Stricter judges raise jailing 13.0 points and cut crime 18.7%; ordering by risk would need only 6.3 points. Second-quintile judges: only 33.2% of extra jailings came from the riskiest 12.0%. National replication: 151,461 felony defendants.
quote: The unobservables create noise, not signal.
limits: Selection-on-observables assumption; judges may weigh other goals than crime; outcomes seen only for released defendants; working paper version.
agent_relevance: Strong case for 'code selects': a simple consistent rule on the same inputs beats the judge. A 'predicted judge' (model of the judge) beats the judge, the same effect as Goldberg 1970.

source: Grove, Zald, Lebow, Snitz, Nelson (2000) meta-analysis of clinical vs mechanical prediction; Meehl (1954) (from memory; PDF blocked, 403)
finding: Across 136 studies, mechanical combination of cues was equal or better than expert clinical judgment in nearly all.
numbers: From memory, to be checked: about 46% of comparisons favoured mechanical, about 48% were ties, about 6% favoured clinical.
limits: NOT OPENED this session. Numbers unverified. Treat as a lead.
agent_relevance: Core of the noise argument: rules remove noise. Check numbers before citing.

source: Goldberg (1970) Man versus model of man (from memory; not opened)
finding: A linear model fitted to a clinician's own judgments predicts the criterion better than the clinician. The model keeps the judge's policy but drops the random error.
numbers: From memory, unverified: in most cases the model of the judge outperformed the judge (MMPI task).
limits: NOT OPENED. Detail unverified.
agent_relevance: Design idea: replace a noisy model step by a fitted rule of its own typical behaviour (code).

source: Danziger, Levav, Avnaim-Pesso (2011) Extraneous factors in judicial decisions, PNAS (from memory; PNAS and PMC blocked)
finding: Israeli parole judges: share of favourable rulings falls within a session and jumps after a break.
numbers: From memory, to be checked: 1,112 rulings, 8 judges; about 65% favourable at session start falling toward 0 before a break.
limits: NOT OPENED. Challenged: Weinshall-Margel and Shapard 2011 (PNAS) argue case order is not random; Glockner 2016 simulation says the effect is overestimated. Treat as contested.
agent_relevance: Occasion noise from fatigue is plausible but this headline study is shaky. LLM analogue: long contexts degrade; test, do not assume.

source: Atil et al. (2025) Non-determinism of 'deterministic' LLM settings, arXiv 2408.04667
finding: Five LLMs, eight tasks (BBH and MMLU subsets), 10 runs each at temperature 0. Accuracy and output text still change between identical runs.
numbers: Accuracy range across runs up to 15%; best-to-worst gap up to 70%. Example: Mixtral-8x7b college math best 75%, worst 3% (72-point gap). Raw-string agreement TARr@10 is often near 0 while parsed-answer agreement TARa@10 is much higher.
quote: Notably, there are 5-15% differences on some tasks.
limits: Answer-extraction code was hand-built; authors say raw outputs may not repeat. Cause (batching, co-mingled inputs) is reported to them by insiders, not shown.
agent_relevance: Occasion noise exists even at temperature 0. One run is one draw. Report ranges; vote or check in code.

source: Atil et al. (2025) - correlations of instability
finding: Instability grows with output length, and agreement rises with accuracy, in the few-shot setting.
numbers: Spearman analysis: strong or moderate negative correlation between output length and TARa@10 and TARr@10; strong positive correlation between median accuracy and TARa@10 (few-shot).
limits: Correlational; eight tasks; five models.
agent_relevance: Long free-form reasoning is a bigger noise source than short constrained answers. Prefer short, checkable slots.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design, ICLR; arXiv 2310.11324
finding: Meaning-preserving changes to prompt format (separators, spacing, casing) change accuracy a lot. This is pattern noise from the prompt.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points for LLaMA-2-13B between equivalent formats; about 10 points on average across 50+ tasks. Median spread 7.5 points over 10 sampled formats; 20% of tasks spread at least 15 points for all LLaMA-2 settings. Not removed by model size, more shots, or instruction tuning.
limits: 10 sampled formats gives a lower bound. Open models; classification tasks mainly.
agent_relevance: A schema prompt is one format draw. Test several paraphrases of each slot instruction before trusting a result.

source: Sclar et al. (2024) - FormatSpread and cross-model correlation
finding: Format performance only weakly correlates between models, so a fixed format does not fairly compare models. FormatSpread uses Bayesian optimisation to estimate the spread cheaply, even for API models.
numbers: GPT-3.5: spread up to 56 points, median 6.4 points over 320 formats and 53 tasks, under 10 USD per task on average.
limits: Cost figure is for their 2023 setup.
agent_relevance: Prompt choice changes model rankings; our scaffold comparisons (plain vs best-of-N vs scaffold) should use several prompt formats.

source: Mizrahi, Kaplan, Malkin, Dror, Shahaf, Stanovsky (2024) State of what art? A call for multi-prompt LLM evaluation; arXiv 2401.00595
finding: Instruction paraphrases change both scores and model rankings.
numbers: 6.5M instances, 20 LLMs, 39 tasks, 3 benchmarks, about 5K paraphrases. Kendall's W (agreement of model ranking across templates) on tasks shown in Table 4: about 0.71 to 0.91, labelled medium to strong, never 1; several tasks have non-significant Friedman p (for example strategic QA W=0.731, p=0.132).
limits: Paraphrases made partly by LLMs; about 85-90% judged correct by humans.
agent_relevance: Single-template benchmark wins can be noise. Our bench harness should report across paraphrases.

source: Lu, Bartolo, Moore, Riedel, Stenetorp (2022) Fantastically ordered prompts, ACL; arXiv 2104.08786
finding: Order of few-shot examples alone moves accuracy from near state of the art to near chance. Good orders do not transfer between models.
numbers: Effect seen from 0.1B up to 175B parameters. Entropy-based selection of orders on a generated dev set gives 13% relative improvement on average across 11 text classification tasks for GPT-family models.
limits: Classification tasks; GPT-2/3 era models.
agent_relevance: Order of items in a prompt is a noise source. Code can shuffle and aggregate over orders.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large language models are not fair evaluators; arXiv 2305.17926
finding: An LLM judge's verdict flips when the order of two responses is swapped. Order alone can crown either model.
numbers: With ChatGPT as judge, Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries (82.5%) in one order. Calibration (3 evidence runs + 3 position-balanced runs) lifts GPT-4 agreement with human labels from 52.7% to 62.5%; adding human review on 20% of items gives 73.8% (human average 71.7%).
limits: 80 queries; one benchmark; GPT-4 and ChatGPT only.
agent_relevance: If any model judge is used, balance positions and aggregate in code (G5). Judge verdicts are noisy.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena; arXiv 2306.05685
finding: LLM judges show position bias: they change verdict when the two answers are swapped.
numbers: Consistency after swapping (default prompt): Claude-v1 23.8%, GPT-3.5 46.2%, GPT-4 65.0%. Claude-v1 favours the first answer 75.0% of the time. A few-shot judge lifts GPT-4 consistency from 65.0% to 77.5%. GPT-4 agrees with humans over 80%.
quote: Only GPT-4 outputs consistent results in more than 60% of cases.
limits: Test pairs built by the authors; 80 questions per judge.
agent_relevance: Even the best judge disagrees with itself in about a third of cases. Judge only with swapped-order pairs and take agreement.

source: Stureborg, Alikaniotis, Suhara (2024) Large language models are inconsistent and biased evaluators; arXiv 2405.01724
finding: GPT-4 as a summary scorer is inconsistent across samples and biased (familiarity/low-perplexity bias, skewed ratings, anchoring on its own previous scores).
numbers: When four attributes are scored in one output, later scores track earlier ones: GPT-4 scores correlate at Pearson r = 0.979 versus humans r = 0.315. Table 4 gives Krippendorff alpha values 0.659 and 0.587; which belongs to humans and which to GPT-4 could not be separated from the text layout.
limits: SummEval and RoSE only; Table 4 reading is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Anchoring on own earlier scores is pure noise; score items independently, each in a fresh call.

source: Ouyang, Zhang, Harman, Wang (2024) Non-determinism of ChatGPT in code generation; arXiv 2308.02828
finding: Same prompt, repeated requests, very different code. Temperature 0 helps but does not remove it.
numbers: 829 problems from CodeContests, APPS, HumanEval. Share of tasks where no two requests gave equal test output: 75.76%, 51.00%, 47.56% at default temperature.
limits: ChatGPT only; default temperature 1.
agent_relevance: Any code-generation step must run tests across several samples, not trust one.

source: Renze (2024) The effect of sampling temperature on problem solving in LLMs; arXiv 2402.05201
finding: Temperature from 0.0 to 1.0 did not significantly change multiple-choice accuracy. Extra sampling noise does not by itself hurt average accuracy, only the reliability of any single run.
numbers: 9 LLMs, 5 prompt techniques, temperature 0.0 to 1.6; CoT on a 1,000-question exam: Kruskal-Wallis H(10)=10.439, p=0.403. Llama 2 7B near random.
limits: Multiple-choice only; mean accuracy is not run-to-run variance. Beyond 1.0 degrades.
agent_relevance: Mean accuracy can be flat while per-item answers flip. Measure agreement, not only accuracy.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning, ICLR; arXiv 2203.11171
finding: Sample many reasoning paths and take the most common final answer. This is the standard noise-averaging step for LLMs.
numbers: Gains over greedy chain of thought: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-c +3.9 points. PaLM-540B GSM8K 56.5 to 74.4. 40 sampled paths, averaged over 10 runs.
limits: Needs a clean final answer to vote on; paths from one model share errors. Gains are small on easy tasks (AddSub +1.8).
agent_relevance: Direct support for G4/G5: voting helps, but agreement among same-model samples is a hint only. Do it in code.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd; arXiv 2402.19379
finding: Median of 12 LLMs matches a human crowd on forecasting; single models do not.
numbers: 31 binary questions vs 925 human forecasters. LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs no-information 0.25, t(30)=-2.35, p=0.026; vs humans 0.19 (SD 0.19), p=0.850. Mean model forecast 57.35% on questions with almost even resolutions (acquiescence bias). Study 2: feeding the median human forecast improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 by 17% to 28%, less than simply averaging.
limits: Only 31 questions; medium-sized equivalence margin; shared biases remain (all models too high).
agent_relevance: Aggregation across different models cancels noise but not shared bias (G4). Diversity of models matters more than count.

source: Synthesis of Atil, Ouyang, Renze and Sclar: three different LLM noise sources
finding: Output-level non-determinism (Atil, Ouyang) is large. Mean accuracy against temperature (Renze) is flat. Prompt-format spread (Sclar) is the largest. These are different noise sources.
numbers: Per-task accuracy ranges up to 15 points across identical runs (Atil) vs no significant mean change with temperature 0-1 (Renze, p=0.403) vs up to 76-point spread across formats (Sclar).
limits: Synthesis across papers read; not a new measurement.
agent_relevance: Order of concern for the scaffold: prompt format and order first, then run-to-run flips, then temperature.

source: Kleinberg et al. (2017) - judge mis-ranking (extra detail from NBER 23180)
finding: Stricter judges do not simply jail the riskiest defendants. Their extra detentions come from across the whole risk range. This is wrong ordering, not only a level shift.
numbers: Stricter-quintile judges raise jailing 13.0 points and cut crime 18.7%; risk-ordered detention would need 6.3 points for the same crime cut.
limits: Same caveats as the main entry.
agent_relevance: Level shifts are cheap to fix; ranking errors need a consistent scoring rule applied by code.

source: Galton (1907) Vox populi; Condorcet jury theorem (from memory; not opened)
finding: Averaging many independent estimates cancels noise but not shared bias.
numbers: From memory, unverified: about 787 usable estimates, median 1,207 lb vs true 1,198 lb.
limits: NOT OPENED. Independence is the key condition and fails for samples from one LLM.
agent_relevance: Foundational reason for G4: samples from one model are correlated, so averaging helps less than averaging independent judges.

source: Kahneman, Sibony, Sunstein (2021) decision hygiene remedies (from memory of the book; not opened)
finding: Remedies named in the book: structure judgments into independent sub-judgments, delay holistic intuition, use anchored scales, aggregate independent judges (mediating assessments protocol).
numbers: No numbers recalled.
limits: NOT OPENED; stated from memory of the book.
agent_relevance: Maps onto our schema: independent sub-judgments in fresh calls, code aggregation, anchored rubrics.

source: Chiang and Lee (2023) Can large language models be an alternative to human evaluation? arXiv 2305.01937 (header checked only)
finding: LLM ratings of text were compared with expert human ratings.
numbers: No numbers extracted this session.
limits: Only the first page was seen; text not read. Do not cite figures.
agent_relevance: Lead for a later pass.
